edits.find:
Bottom line
  • A lifelong pattern, present by early adulthood and generally stable across settings; instability that comes in episodes with a start and an end points to a mood disorder
  • Borderline: abandonment fear, unstable relationships and self-image, self-harm, and transient stress-related paranoia lasting minutes to hours; first-line treatment is psychotherapy, with the best evidence for dialectical behavior therapy
  • Antisocial needs age 18 or older and conduct disorder before 15; under 18, antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed; consider conduct disorder

edits.find:
Bottom line
  • Anticholinergic signs or any tricyclic overdose: an ECG (electrocardiogram) first; a QRS over 100 ms, a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension calls for sodium bicarbonate
  • Agitation or seizures: a benzodiazepine. No haloperidol; no physostigmine once a tricyclic is involved
  • QRS width, not pupil size, bowel sounds or a drug level, predicts seizures and arrhythmia

edits.find:
Bottom line
  • 2 or more motor tics 1 or more vocal tics, at least 1 year, onset before 18 Tourette syndrome; echolalia counts as vocal
  • Repeated act no obsession behind it a tic, not a compulsion
  • No impairment explain and watch. Impairment CBIT (comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics) medication: a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter type 2) inhibitor such as tetrabenazine first, or an antipsychotic; an alpha-2 agonist for milder tics, especially with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder)

edits.find:
Bottom line
  • Stabilize first: airway and breathing, a fingerstick glucose and an ECG (electrocardiogram); naloxone for slow breathing with pinpoint pupils
  • In every intentional overdose, check acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and suspect more than one substance
  • Then name the toxidrome from the pupils, the skin, the bowel sounds and the muscle tone
